newsitem.title: UK: Past U.N. peacekeeping efforts had mixed success.
newsitem.headline: Past U.N. peacekeeping efforts had mixed success.

text.p: The United Nations is expected on Friday to give its blessing to a multinational force for Zaire but similar U.N. missions have enjoyed mixed success in the past.
Some of the major previous U.N. missions include:

THE CONGO - In 1960 the United Nations sent a 20,000-strong force to quell fighting sparked by the end of Belgian colonial rule in the newly-dependent African state of Zaire, previously called the Congo. The situation worsened when army chief of staff Joseph Mobutu overthrew Prime Minister Patrice Lumumba, prompting the Security Council to authorise its troops to use force to prevent a civil war. Six nations later withdrew their forces in protest after Mobutu's forces executed Lumumba. The U.N.-force managed to disarm most of the warring groups but had to battle on until January 1963 when rebels in the southern Katanga province laid down their arms. U.N. losses totalled 237, including 44 Ghanians who were killed in one day in 1961. The conflict also cost the life of U.N. Secretary-General Dag Hammarskjold, killed in a plane crash in September 1961 as he flew to meet the head of the Katanga rebels. The U.N. troops left in June 1964.

The United Nations was badly stung by its mission in the former Yugoslavia, widely claimed to be one of the least successful peacekeeping operations of modern times. In 1992 the U.N. sent its UNPROFOR protection force to guard Serb-inhabited areas in Croatia and then to Bosnia-Herzegovina to escort relief supplies. Around 22,000 troops and police were deployed but the force was criticised for being ineffective, since its mandate prevented it from taking action against the Bosnian Serb forces attacking Sarajevo. In May 1995 Serb forces took hundreds of peacekeepers hostage in retaliation for limited NATO air strikes and in July captured Srebrenica, which was supposed to be a U.N. "safe area", in one of the most horrific episodes of the war. Thousands of Moslem men went missing, believed to have been killed and buried in mass graves, and Dutch U.N. forces on the ground were accused of doing nothing to stop the Serbs. In late August Western forces mounted a series of air strikes until the Serbs agreed to attend peace talks. The U.N. transferred authority for the peace mission to NATO in December 1995. More than 100 U.N. peacekeepers and civilian workers were killed.

In December 1992 the U.N. authorised the United States to deploy 38,000 troops in Somalia to prevent mass starvation. In May 1993 the United Nations' UNOSOM force took over from the U.S troops but found itself locked into fighting with local warlord Mohamed Farah Aideed. On June 5 1993, 23 Pakistani soldiers were killed in fighting with Aideed's forces and the U.N. mission was dealt a fatal blow when 18 U.S. rangers sent to hunt down Aideed were killed in Mogadishu. The remaining U.S. forces withdrew and the U.N. mandate ended in March 1995 when its last troops pulled out, leaving the local warlords to fight on. The U.N. suffered further loss of face when it was revealed that Canadian troops on U.N. duty had tortured and killed several Somalis in 1992 and 1993. At least 135 U.N. personnel were killed during the ill-fated mission.

The U.N. Peacekeeping Force in Cyprus (UNFICYP) was set up in 1964 to help stop fighting between the island's ethnic Greek and Turkish communities. The force was helpless to prevent a Turkish invasion in 1974 but since then has managed to maintain the peace. The 1,50-strong contingent of U.N. troops controls a 180 km (112 mile) buffer zone across the island which was set up the invasion. A small army of mediators working under United Nations auspices for more than 20 years to reunite the island as a bicommunal federation have failed to achieve any progress. Around 160 U.N. personnel have been killed so far.
